data.name: The Adventurer and His Backpack
data.detailed_description:
The game is just a self-developed small relaxing game, please do not expect too much from it. In my point of view, as long as the current game is better than the previous, I have achieved my objective.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The adventure game style is tilted more to the quirky side with different game modes resulting in different objectives but the overall game style will stay the same.
This game has a seed generation mode which will enable players to share and compete against each other, just enter the seed generated.

Instructions：
1.Use the left mouse button to move items between the equipment menu and the backpack.
2.Use the right mouse button to use consumables.
3.Click on the backpack button to raise its panel to view the backpack inventory.
4.The game ends immediately upon death, each different game mode has its own score calculation.
5.There're 3 choices upon meeting a monster:
·Attack —— Attack the monster, might land a critical hit or dodged by the monster, speed will be the factor to determine who attacks first.
·Escape —— The success rate is determined by the speed difference, a successful escape will grant no rewards and move on to the next day.
·Settle with gold coins —— Use a certain amount of gold coins to win and get the rewards without combat. The amount of gold coins required is the total sum of the rewards' purchase price.
6.You'll find a shop every 10 days, hold down the keyboard CTRL button and click with the left mouse button to sell. Items can only be sold at the shop.

Stats Related：
1.Normal Damage Calculation —— （Physical attack of attacker - physical defense of target） + （Magical attack of attacker - magical defense of target） = Normal Damage. Which means that both physical and magical damage will be dealt when applicable.
2.Swapping equipment will not reduce current health points, rest assure while swapping.
3.The type of property from each obtainable equipment will not change, but the value of the property will scale according to progress.
4.Each type of monster has its own unique property which will scale according to progress.

data.short_description: This is a turn-based relaxing adventure game with simple controls. You play as an adventurer, bringing a backpack with limited number of slots, who goes on an adventure. You will meet different kinds of monsters, defeat them, strengthen yourself to face stronger monsters. Be the ultimate adventurer!

reviews.review:
The Adventurer and His Backpack is a compact turn-based adventure that builds its identity around survival, inventory limitations, equipment choices, and the constant question of whether an encounter is worth the risk. Developed by 疯王子 and published by CrazyPrince, it carries the unmistakable character of a small independent project. Rather than attempting to deliver an enormous RPG campaign, it concentrates on a repeatable progression loop where careful resource management can be just as important as winning battles.

The central adventure revolves around surviving a sequence of increasingly dangerous encounters. Monsters grow stronger as progress continues, meaning equipment that feels adequate early in a run may eventually become insufficient. Combat takes physical and magical attributes into account, with offensive statistics working against their corresponding defenses. Speed is another important consideration because it can influence how encounters unfold and becomes particularly valuable when attempting to escape. The mechanics are relatively easy to understand, but the gradual increase in enemy strength gives players a reason to continually reconsider their equipment and overall preparedness.

One of the better aspects of the encounter system is that combat is not always mandatory. Fighting offers the obvious opportunity to defeat an enemy and claim rewards, but it also exposes the adventurer to potentially run-ending damage. Escaping provides an alternative when the situation looks unfavorable, although success depends partly on speed. Players can also use gold to resolve certain encounters rather than fighting. This turns money into more than a simple shopping currency because preserving gold must be weighed against preserving health and keeping the run alive.

The backpack is where many of the game's most meaningful decisions occur. Inventory capacity is restricted, preventing players from simply collecting every potentially useful object. Equipment, consumables, and other valuable possessions compete for limited space, so deciding what to keep becomes part of the strategy. A weaker item might be worth discarding immediately, while another object could be carried until it can eventually be sold. The resulting inventory management is uncomplicated but effective because almost every slot has an opportunity cost.

Shops provide another layer to this resource-management loop. They appear periodically rather than remaining permanently accessible, giving players specific opportunities to buy supplies and sell unwanted possessions. This arrangement makes planning important. Carrying unnecessary equipment until the next shop consumes valuable backpack space, but abandoning it means losing the gold that could have been earned from selling it. Meanwhile, spending too much money on upgrades can leave fewer resources available for avoiding particularly dangerous encounters. These small tradeoffs form much of the game's strategic appeal.

Permanent failure adds tension to otherwise straightforward mechanics. Once the adventurer dies, the current attempt ends, encouraging players to learn from unsuccessful runs and approach future encounters more cautiously. Different modes offer varying goals and scoring considerations, helping the experience function as something of a score-chasing game rather than a conventional narrative RPG. Seed generation also provides an interesting feature by allowing particular adventure configurations to be reproduced, which makes comparing runs under similar circumstances possible.

The game also offers a surprisingly substantial collection of achievements, with 98 available for players interested in completion goals. Steam Trading Cards and Steam Cloud functionality add some additional platform integration. These features do not fundamentally transform the experience, but they fit well with a game designed around repeated attempts. Achievement hunters in particular may find an additional incentive to experiment with mechanics or continue playing after becoming familiar with the basic progression.

Presentation is considerably more modest than the underlying collection of mechanics. This is not a visually elaborate dungeon crawler filled with cinematic sequences, detailed character performances, or expansive environments. Its independent origins are readily apparent, and some players may find the presentation rough or minimal. The straightforward visual approach does at least keep attention focused on statistics, inventory decisions, and encounters rather than distracting from the central gameplay systems.

The largest limitation is repetition. Combat relies substantially on numerical relationships rather than an enormous selection of tactical actions, while backpack management is primarily concerned with prioritizing limited space instead of creating extremely elaborate equipment combinations. Once players understand how encounters, statistics, shops, gold, equipment, and inventory capacity interact, there may not be enough additional complexity to satisfy anyone seeking a deeply layered roguelike or RPG. The experience is better suited to players who appreciate relatively simple systems working together within short, repeatable runs.

Steam Deck compatibility is less definitive. The game does not have an official Valve Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation, so it should be regarded as Steam Deck compatibility unknown rather than confirmed. Its relatively simple interface and lightweight nature may make experimentation through Proton possible, but that should not be confused with official compatibility. Players specifically purchasing it for handheld use should therefore expect that manual adjustments, alternative control input, or other workarounds could potentially be necessary.

Taken on its own terms, The Adventurer and His Backpack is an interesting little exercise in balancing risk, resources, equipment, money, and limited inventory capacity. Its strongest quality is how several simple mechanics reinforce one another: fighting can provide rewards but costs health, escaping preserves survival at the expense of progress opportunities, paying consumes valuable money, and carrying items consumes backpack space. None of these concepts is especially complicated individually, yet together they produce decisions that can matter considerably during a successful run. Its limited production values and repetitive structure prevent it from becoming an essential dungeon-crawling experience, but there is enough personality and mechanical thought here to make it worthwhile for players who enjoy compact indie adventures built around repeated attempts and resource optimization.

Rating: 6/10
